topic.title: The Gauge Said Normal. The Tower Was Nearly Full.

title: The Gauge Said Normal. The Tower Was Nearly Full.
description:
One March morning a distillation tower at the BP Texas City refinery was started up after maintenance. Its level gauge said the liquid was low. It was nearly at the top.
We rebuild the unit in 3D and follow the U.S. Chemical Safety Board's investigation: a tower filled for hours with nothing taken out, a gauge that could only see the bottom of it, an old vent stack with no flare, and trailers parked close by.
Then what the board found, and what it asked the industry to change.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
0:41 The Unit
1:42 The Start-up
2:56 The Gauge
3:47 The Overflow
5:02 The Blast
6:03 The Findings
7:04 What Changed

Source: U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, Refinery Explosion and Fire, BP Texas City (final report).
Based on official investigation reports and published sources. 3D scenes are reconstructions, not actual footage.

Report: US Chemical Safety Board, CSB Investigation Report: Refinery Explosion and Fire, BP Texas City, page 18 of 341, Public domain (US government work) (https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/20/CSBFinalReportBP.pdf?13841)

lines.text: Texas City, March 23, 2005. A refinery tower 170 feet tall is being started up after maintenance.
In the control room, its level gauge says the liquid sits near the bottom.
In fact, the liquid is almost at the top.
It pours out through relief valves, fills an old vent stack, and erupts into the air like a geyser.
It wasn't one failure. It was a gauge that couldn't see, a vent with no flare, and trailers parked too close.
Here is the unit, the start-up, the gauge, the overflow, the blast, the findings, and what changed.
The BP refinery at Texas City was the third largest in the United States.
Its isomerization unit turned refinery streams into high octane blending stock for gasoline.
Nearby, contract workers were using temporary trailers, set up for maintenance work on another unit.
At its heart stood the raffinate splitter, a distillation tower 170 feet tall.
How does a splitter work? A furnace heats the liquid, the light part boils up the tower, and the heavy part is drawn off at the bottom.
Inside, stacked trays split the liquid into a light part and a heavy part.
Normally, only the bottom few feet of the tower held liquid.
How did anyone know the level? A level transmitter watched the liquid. But it could only see the bottom 9 feet.
Above that line, the gauge was blind. On March 23, that blind spot would matter.
The unit had been shut down for maintenance. Now crews were starting it up again.
The night operator began filling the tower with liquid before dawn.
He stopped when the gauge read near the top of its range. One high level alarm sounded. The backup alarm never did.
The start-up procedure said to fill it only to 50% on the gauge.
Was going past the gauge unusual? No. In 15 of the 19 start-ups the board studied, the level went beyond its range.
The operators had been working twelve hour shifts for 29 or more days in a row.
Who was watching? One board operator, running three units from the same console.
Mid-morning, the day crew restarted the feed and lit the furnace burners.
Liquid kept flowing in. But the valve that takes liquid out stayed shut.
For over 3 hours, the tower filled and almost nothing left it.
Late in the morning, the supervisor left for a family emergency. No one trained took his place.
On the board, the level looked fine. In the tower, it was climbing.
What did the operators see, and what was really in the tower?
Late morning, the gauge still showed a low level. The real level was 67 feet.
Before noon, it was 98 feet.
Early afternoon, 140 feet.
Then 158 feet, in a tower 170 feet tall. And the gauge showed the level falling.
Why? The transmitter was set up for the bottom of the tower, and calibrated for a liquid of a different density.
Could they look inside? The only window was a sight glass on the tower. It had been unreadable for years.
Minutes later, a safety meeting began in the main control room.
With the tower nearly full, the liquid had one way left to go: over the top.
What happens when a tower overfills?
At the top, liquid spilled into the overhead pipe, which ran back down the side of the tower.
At the bottom of that pipe, 148 feet down, sat three pressure relief valves.
As the pipe filled with liquid, the pressure there rose from about 21 to about 64 psi.
The relief valves did their job and opened. For 6 minutes, they stayed open.
They sent about 51,900 gallons of flammable liquid to the blowdown drum.
The drum and its stack were decades old, and vented straight to the open air.
It had never been connected to a flare, which would have burned the vapour off safely.
In 1992, a federal inspector had cited a similar drum and stack as unsafe. The citation was later withdrawn.
The drum overfilled. Liquid erupted from the top of the 113 foot stack, like a geyser.
The liquid was so volatile that it turned to vapour as it fell.
And 25 feet from the drum, a pickup truck sat idling, its engine running.
Where did it go? A cloud of flammable vapour spread along the ground, toward the trailers.
At 20 past 1 in the afternoon, it found an ignition source.
What lit it? The most likely source, the board found, was the idling diesel pickup truck.
Then, in an instant, the whole cloud ignited.
The blast tore through the trailers parked near the unit.
Some had been placed as close as 121 feet from the blowdown drum.
More than 40 trailers were damaged. 13 were destroyed.
A person in a trailer was injured as far as 479 feet away.
15 people died. All of them were in or near those trailers. 180 were injured.
Around the refinery, 43,000 people were told to stay indoors.
Why were people in trailers so close to a unit starting up? The board asked that too.
The U.S. Chemical Safety Board investigated. Its finding was blunt.
The disaster was caused by organizational and safety deficiencies at all levels of the company.
Why did it happen? The board traced it link by link.
Liquid was fed in for over 3 hours with none taken out, against the start-up procedure.
Instruments and alarms gave false readings, and the operators were likely tired and poorly trained.
And there was no requirement to pass on the state of the start-up from one shift to the next.
Warning signs had been there for years, the board wrote, but company officials did not step in effectively.
The blowdown stack was an unsafe design, kept in service despite earlier warnings.
And occupied trailers had been placed too close to a unit handling highly hazardous materials.
So what changed after Texas City?
Did anything change? Months before its final report, the board issued urgent recommendations.
It asked the American Petroleum Institute to write new guidelines to keep occupied trailers away from hazardous process areas.
The institute agreed. And the board called for an alert urging companies to act promptly to place their trailers safely.
And the vent stack? The board asked the institute to revise its guide on relief systems, naming the hazards of blowdown drums and urging safer alternatives.
The last reading before the blast: the gauge said the level was falling. The tower held 158 feet of liquid.
A blind gauge. A tower filled for hours. A stack with no flare. Trailers too close.

thumbnails.why: Credible and on-brand, but a page of text is harder to read small than the eruption or the gauges.
